notes:
I've written notes on all 26 verses, but some parts of the research are thin. My tool access ran out partway through, so I only read a limited set of sources:

- **Read in full:** Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott's Commentary (vv. 1–17 only; the page cut off after that), and the NET Bible notes.
- **Read from the excerpts shown in search results:** the Catholic Encyclopedia articles on Cain and Abel, St. Basil's Letter 260, Augustine's *City of God* XV, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin, Constable, the Biblical Illustrator, and Bible Hub's Genesis 4:4 page.
- **Not reached:** Gill, the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley, any Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox site, Bible Odyssey, Got Questions, and anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those topics are left out.

Because of that, section 2 can't set out what each Protestant tradition says in its own teachers' words. Instead, under each verse I note where the commentators I read disagree.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- "Knew" is the Bible's polite word for sex. Guzik says it shows sex as something that builds the one-flesh bond, and he sees no reason to think Adam and Eve had no sex before this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Guzik thinks Eve probably believed Cain was the promised "seed" of Genesis 3:15, the Messiah, when in fact she was holding a future murderer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Ellicott reads the Hebrew as "I have gotten a man, *even* Jehovah." He says Eve was pointing to the promise of a coming deliverer, not claiming her baby was divine. He also allows a simpler sense: the child showed the human race would survive death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- Matthew Henry says only that Eve "perhaps" thought Cain was the promised seed, and if so she was badly disappointed. He takes the name Cain to mean "possession." https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-4-commentary
- The NET notes point to wordplay: the verb *qanah* ("I have created/gotten") sounds like the name Cain. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4
- The Catholic Encyclopedia also connects the name to *kanah*, "to possess." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03142b.htm

**v. 2**
- Abel's name (*hevel*) means "breath" or "vapour." The NET notes hear it as a hint of his early death. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4
- Ellicott thinks the name was probably given only after Abel died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- Henry reads the name as "vanity": Eve was so taken with Cain that a second son seemed like nothing to her. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_004.cfm
- Guzik takes the two jobs as evidence that farming and herding go back to the very first humans. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Ellicott contrasts the two brothers' characters. He notes that Adam was 130 when Seth was born, which leaves time for many other children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia's Abel article lists several proposed meanings of the name, from "son" to "sorrow" to "herdsman." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01035c.htm

**v. 3**
- The NET notes say the word for offering (*minchah*) means any gift or tribute and could include vegetables. The offerer's attitude mattered, not the contents. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=gen+4:3-5
- Ellicott warns against reading later Levitical laws into this offering. He takes "in the course of time" to mean a long, open-ended period. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- Guzik guesses the brothers may have brought their offerings to the cherubim at the tree of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/

**vv. 4–5 (the best-known disagreement)**
- **The traditional answer is faith (Hebrews 11:4).** Guzik, Ellicott, the NET notes and the Catholic Encyclopedia all give this reason.
  - Guzik notes that grain offerings were acceptable to God (Leviticus 2), though not to atone for sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Ellicott says the state of the brothers' hearts made the difference. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - The NET notes say the same. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Gen&chapter=4&verse=5&tab=commentaries&theme=wiki
- **Some say it was the quality of the gift.** The NET notes describe Cain as simply doing his duty, while Abel went out of his way to give the first and best. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Gen&chapter=4&verse=4&tab=commentaries&theme=wiki
  - One commentary excerpted on Bible Hub (the excerpt doesn't name its author) says the blood-versus-grain difference just came from their jobs. The real point was that Abel brought the fattest firstlings and Cain did not bring firstfruits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/4-4.htm
- **Others say it was a blood sacrifice for sin.** Another excerpt on the same page says Abel brought an atoning sacrifice, confessing himself a sinner. Cain's was only an offering of thanks to the Creator. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/4-4.htm
  - The Biblical Illustrator says the same: Cain's offering was a thank-offering, Abel's was an atoning one. It adds that "the free grace of God" is the root cause of the difference. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-4.html
- **Ellicott takes a middle position.** Abel's animal sacrifice may have shown deeper faith in the promised Deliverer. Cain's bloodless offering later became the grain offering of the Law, and in the Christian era prayer, praise and the Eucharistic thanksgiving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- **On the person behind the gift,** Henry says God did not regard Cain himself, so he did not regard his offering. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_004.cfm
- Constable sets out both views: that Abel's attitude showed his faith, and that his faith showed in bringing the best. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-4.html
- **How did they know God's verdict?**
  - Guzik and Henry suggest fire from heaven consumed Abel's offering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_004.cfm
  - Ellicott calls adding this detail to the story irreverent. It is enough that the brothers knew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - The NET notes leave it open: an outward sign or an inner awareness. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=gen+4:3-5
- **Catholic reading.** The Encyclopedia says the text does not give the reason. It cites Augustine (Cain gave God some of his goods but not his heart), 1 John 3:12 and Hebrews 11:4. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03142b.htm
  - The Abel article says Abel gave with generosity and love, and cites Josephus's different view. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01035c.htm
- **Cain's anger.** Guzik traces it to pride and spiritual jealousy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - The NET notes say "his face fell" shows inner anger or dejection, the opposite of the Lord "lifting up his face" in the priestly blessing. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=gen+4:3-5

**v. 6**
- Guzik: God already knew the answers. He was confronting Cain in love, to help him resist the pull toward anger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Ellicott: God still spoke with Cain as kindly as he once had with Adam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm

**v. 7**
- **Common reading.** Sin is pictured as a beast crouching at the door, eager for Cain, and Cain must master it.
  - Guzik: we keep sin from ruling us by letting God master us first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says the same and stresses that Cain was able to resist. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03142b.htm
- **NET notes.** The question is meant as encouragement, not condemnation. The hard Hebrew word means "lifting up," the opposite of a fallen face. "You must subdue it" can also mean "you are able to master it." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+4:1-16&lang=de/1000
- **Ellicott's alternative.** He points out that the pronouns are masculine while "sin" is feminine. So he prefers this reading: if Cain does well, his *brother's* desire will be toward him and Cain will rule over him, regaining his rights as firstborn (compare Genesis 3:16). He sees a real struggle in Cain's conscience, with repentance still possible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm

**v. 8**
- **Text.** The ancient versions add "Let us go out to the field," which the standard Hebrew text lacks.
  - Ellicott says the versions carry real weight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - The NET notes suggest a scribe's eye skipped those words by accident. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+4:1-16&lang=de/1000
- **Was it planned?**
  - Guzik: yes. Cain disarmed Abel with friendly talk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Basil counts "guile" in the invitation as one of Cain's seven sins. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202260.htm
  - Ellicott: no. Cain didn't yet know what human death was. He imagines a shepherd–farmer quarrel that got out of hand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- The NET notes point out that "brother" appears six times in vv. 8–11, stressing how shocking the killing was. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+4:1-16&lang=de/1000
- Augustine: Cain killed out of the hatred the wicked feel toward the good. He links this murder with Romulus killing Remus. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120115.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: God asked so that Cain could confess. In fact he *was* meant to be his brother's keeper. Guzik quotes Spurgeon on Cain's "cool impudence" and ties this to "the way of Cain" (Jude 11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Basil: the question was asked to give Cain a chance to repent. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202260.htm
- Henry: Cain covered a deliberate murder with a deliberate lie. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_004.cfm
- The NET notes compare God's questions to Adam in Genesis 3:9–13. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4

**v. 10**
- Guzik, Ellicott and Henry all contrast this verse with Hebrews 12:24. Abel's blood cried for justice and vengeance; Christ's blood speaks of pardon and peace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_004.cfm
- Guzik links the verse to Numbers 35, where unpunished bloodshed defiles the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik: Adam's curse is made stronger for Cain. Farming becomes impossible for him, and he finds no place to rest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Ellicott: Cain was the first human to be cursed directly, and the ground he polluted now resists him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- The NET notes and the Catholic Encyclopedia both say the Hebrew can mean either "cursed *by* the ground" or "cursed and banished *from* the ground." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+4:1-16&lang=de/1000 ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03142b.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- The Hebrew word can mean "sin," "guilt" or "punishment."
  - The NET notes take "punishment" here and add that Cain is not shown repenting. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4
  - Ellicott gives the full sense as "my sin is past forgiveness, and its result is an intolerable punishment." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- Guzik: Cain was sorry about his punishment, not his sin. He cites Boice and Barnhouse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- **"Whoever finds me will kill me."** Ellicott lists three views: Adam's other sons; earlier, lesser races of people; or simply an empty fear on Cain's part. He prefers the last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- Basil gives the Greek reading "groaning and trembling" and treats it as bodily punishment. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202260.htm

**v. 15**
- **Sevenfold.**
  - The NET notes say seven is a symbolic number for severe punishment, and that here God becomes Cain's protector, an act of common grace without salvation. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+4:1-16&lang=de/1000
  - Ellicott: seven stands for complete vengeance. He sees the beginning of the later cities of refuge here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - Guzik suggests God spared Cain partly because there were so few people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Basil: Cain committed seven sins, and the one who kills him carries out the sevenfold sentence. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202260.htm
- **The mark.**
  - Guzik: nobody knows what it was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Ellicott: it wasn't a brand on his body. It was an appointed sign, like the rainbow given to Noah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - NET notes: some visible reminder of his protection, though the text doesn't say what. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4

**v. 16**
- "Nod" means "wandering." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=4
- Ellicott: Cain thought he had moved beyond God's sight. Ellicott also lists guesses about where Nod was, with little confidence in any of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm

**v. 17**
- **Cain's wife.**
  - Guzik: she was his sister (Genesis 5:4). This came before the Mosaic ban on such marriages; Abraham also married his half-sister. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Ellicott: she was one of Adam's daughters who followed Cain into exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
- **The city.**
  - Guzik: naming it after his son shows a man-centred start to city life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
  - Ellicott: "Enoch" means "dedicated" or "trained," which may show that Cain's character softened. The Hebrew says he "was building" (began to build) a city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm
  - Augustine: Cain built a city, but Abel, as a pilgrim, built none. The two brothers stand for the earthly city and the city of God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120115.htm ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01035c.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Lamech was the seventh generation from Adam through Cain (counting Adam). Godly Enoch was the seventh through Seth (Jude 14). Guzik's page says "sixth," but by its own list both are seventh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/

**v. 19**
- Guzik: Lamech was the first man with two wives, against God's design in Genesis 2:24. He reads the women's names as showing a culture devoted to outward beauty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/

**vv. 20–22**
- NET notes: "father" here means founder, the first to take up that way of life. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Gen&chapter=4&verse=20
- Guzik: progress came fast, in tents, music and metalworking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Ellicott: Cain's godless line pulled far ahead of Seth's in the arts of civilisation, which eased the curse of labour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/4.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- NET notes: Lamech misunderstands God's mercy to Cain. God was trying to *limit* bloodshed, and Lamech wants to multiply it. "Seventy-seven" is deliberate exaggeration. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php/verse.php?book=Gen&chapter=4&verse=24
- Guzik: Lamech's boast shows humanity sliding further down, and neither he nor his descendants are heard of again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Basil appears to speak in Lamech's voice: having seen Cain punished, he deserved far more punishment himself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202260.htm

**v. 25**
- Guzik: Seth replaces Abel and carries forward the promise of Genesis 3:15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Catholic Encyclopedia: since Eve calls Seth a replacement for Abel, Abel probably had no descendants, or none still alive. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01035c.htm

**v. 26**
- Guzik: true worship survived even in wicked times. Some call this verse "the first revival." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-4/
- Wenham (quoted by Precept Austin): "call on the name of the LORD" covers worship in general, such as prayer and sacrifice. The verse marks the start of *regular* worship, just as the verses before it mark the start of farming, music and metalwork. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-4-commentary

---

**Other views, in brief**
- **Modern scholarship:** the NET notes' work on the text and wording (vv. 7, 8, 13). Constable cites Wenham on how this chapter mirrors the structure of Genesis 2–3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-4.html
- **Catholic and patristic:** Augustine's "two cities" and his view of Abel as a type of the reborn person, Basil's "seven sins," and the old tradition of fire from heaven.
  - The Abel article also mentions later Jewish and Islamic legends, such as a raven showing how to bury Abel. These are traditions, not part of Genesis. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01035c.htm
- **Not found:** Orthodox sources, and any of the debated popular modern teachings.
